platforms.title: Which platforms to choose
platforms.content: Facebook fits broad demographics, longer posts, and events. Instagram fits visual storytelling. Start with one platform and do it well. Many locals rely on a closed Facebook group.

tone.title: Tone of voice
tone.content: Professional but human. Speak as a collective (“we”, “our members”). Celebrate wins, explain setbacks honestly, and centre member voices. Avoid jargon: write for a phone screen on break.

frequency.title: Posting frequency
frequency.content: Aim for 2-3 posts per week in normal times; increase during bargaining or strike. Consistency beats volume. Simple mix: 40% updates, 30% member stories, 20% education, 10% solidarity.

trolls.title: Dealing with trolls and management
trolls.content: Do not engage bad-faith comments. Hide or delete spam, harassment, and misinformation. For management pushback, stick to facts, cite the CA, and escalate. Never post confidential bargaining details.

accessibility.title: Accessibility - alt-text
accessibility.content: Every image needs alt text. Draft with Alt-Text Assistant, paste into the platform field (not the caption). Cover who, what, where, and on-image text.

unionBoardsGuide.title: Union Boards Guide
unionBoardsGuide.subtitle: Reach members who are not on social. Start with a bare-minimum layout, then add notices and posters.

bareMinimum.title: Bare-minimum board
bareMinimum.intro: Every board should answer: How do I find you online? Who do I call for health and safety? Who is on the LEC? What is happening next?
bareMinimum.tip: Print always-on pieces once on sturdy stock. Refresh only the rotating zone. Fill empty space with solidarity posters so the board never looks abandoned.

header.title: Local header
header.content: Local number, short name, and Brand Kit logo. Print a Board Banner so the cork reads as yours from across the room.

socials.title: Socials and digital link
socials.content: Add one QR code or short URL that points to your site, your group, or this site. One clear call to action (“Get support” or “Follow us”) beats a wall of icons.

healthSafety.title: Health and safety
healthSafety.content: JHSC / H&S contacts, how to report a hazard, and where to find the latest bulletin. Keep phone numbers large and current.

lec.title: LEC and steward list
lec.content: Local Executive Committee roles with names and work contacts (or steward office hours). Update after elections - outdated lists erode trust.

events.title: Events or rotating spot
events.content: Membership meetings, bargaining updates, workshops, or a solidarity poster. This is the only zone that should change weekly.

whatToPrint.title: What to print
whatToPrint.intro: Think in layers: permanent identity, standing resources, and a rotating slot.

always.label: Always on the board
always.content: Header/logo, socials QR or URL, health & safety contacts, LEC / steward list.

rotate.label: Rotate often
rotate.content: Meeting notices, bargaining updates, event flyers, and high-energy solidarity posters for empty space.

optional.label: Optional extras
optional.content: Member spotlight (with consent), contract highlight one-pagers, how-to-file-a-grievance tear-offs.

sizes.label: Sizes that work
sizes.content: Letter (8.5×11) for dense contact lists; tabloid (11×17) for notices and posters readable from across the room.

where.title: Where to post
where.content: Use union-designated boards in break rooms, steward offices, and agreed spots. Never post on management boards without permission. Check CA posting rights.

howLong.title: How long to leave notices up
howLong.content: Remove outdated notices promptly. Meetings: post 1-2 weeks ahead, remove after. Bargaining: refresh weekly. Strike: daily. Keep bare-minimum zones current.

whatNot.title: What not to post
whatNot.content: Never post confidential bargaining positions, member home addresses, or internal strategy. Do not name individuals in grievances. Ask your president if unsure.

pairing.title: Pair with social media
pairing.content: Use the same headline on the board notice and social graphic. Post the board first, then share on social with a photo of the posted notice (consent anyone visible).

printGuide.title: Print Communications Guide
printGuide.subtitle: Why print still matters, how to design flyers that work, and how to print on a local budget.
printGuide.intro: Paper still reaches members who never see a post. Use this page to decide when to print, how to design for the shop floor, and how to stretch a small budget.

when.title: When to print
when.intro: Print is not a backup for locals that feel behind on digital. It is how you reach people social media never sees, and how you make the union visible in the workplace itself.

divide.label: It bridges the digital divide
divide.content: Not every member has a smartphone, a data plan, or quiet time to scroll. A flyer in the hand or a notice by the time clock does not need a login.

offline.label: It reaches members who skip social media
offline.content: Many members mute work-adjacent groups, never joined the local page, or do not use Facebook or Instagram at all. Print still finds them on the floor.

presence.label: It is a physical reminder the union is here
presence.content: A posted notice is hard to swipe away. It tells everyone walking past that this local is present in the workplace, not only online.

when.tip: If the message matters and the room is mixed — different shifts, languages, or comfort with phones — print it. Flyers for rallies and walkabouts; board notices for ongoing visibility.

flyers.title: Flyers and handouts
flyers.intro: Use Flyer Maker for picket lines, rallies, membership meetings, and walkabouts, then export a PDF for letter, half-letter, or tabloid printing. The tool carries your Brand Kit colours and local number so the stack looks like you.

glance.label: Glance Test
glance.content: Can a member understand the main point in three seconds, from arm's length? If not, enlarge the headline or cut copy until they can.

words.label: Keep the word count low
words.content: Aim for a short headline, a few lines of body, and the facts (what, when, where). If you need a paragraph, the flyer is doing a newsletter's job. Cut it.

action.label: One clear call to action
action.content: Ask for one next step: show up, scan the code, talk to a steward, or share with a coworker. Two asks on one flyer means neither gets done.

qr.label: QR codes bridge print and digital
qr.content: Point the code at your local website, a membership form, or an Officer Hub RSVP link. Paper gives the facts; the scan gives the live page if details change.

type.label: Large, high-contrast type
type.content: Hallways, parking lots, and picket lines are not desks. Keep the text large and dark on a light field (or the reverse) so it still reads outdoors.

flyers.tip: Print one proof and do the Glance Test in a hallway, not at your desk. Test every QR on a phone before you print a stack.

boards.title: Board notices
boards.intro: Use Board Notice Maker for workplace corks. Tabloid (11×17) reads from farther away. Letter (8.5×11) fits most standard boards. Pair this page with the Union Boards Guide for layout, zones, and what to keep up year-round.

place.label: Put boards where members already stop
place.content: Break rooms, time clocks, and the entrance people actually use beat a quiet corridor. If you have more than one site, give each site a board you can keep current.

expired.label: Take down expired notices
expired.content: A meeting flyer still up a week later makes the union look asleep. Pull it the day after, and keep standing pieces (contacts, health and safety, how to find you) current.

agreement.label: Check your collective agreement
agreement.content: Employer rules for union boards live in your collective agreement and any posting policy. Some workplaces only allow union materials on designated boards.

boards.warning: Do not tape a flyer to a door, window, or management board unless your collective agreement or a written posting practice allows it. When you are unsure, ask your president or steward before you post.

logistics.title: Printing logistics and tips
logistics.intro: Most locals print on a tight budget, often on a workplace copier. Design for the machine you actually have, then spend colour money only when the run is official.

bw.label: Design for black and white
bw.content: Colour ink is expensive, and many shop copiers only do greyscale. If the flyer still reads without colour, it will also read in colour — and it will survive a cheap copy.

contrast.label: Keep text contrast high
contrast.content: Pale grey on white fails on a tired copier and in a dim hallway. Dark text on a light field (or the reverse) is the difference between a notice people read and one they walk past.

union.label: Use a unionized print shop when the run is big
union.content: Home and copy-shop letter printing is fine for a meeting stack. For bulk runs or official campaign printing, prefer a unionized print shop when one is available.

proof.label: Print one proof first
proof.content: Letter (8.5×11) is the cheapest stack; tabloid (11×17) is worth it for boards that must read from across a room. Read the proof at arm's length in hallway light before you copy fifty.

logistics.tip: Recycled or slightly heavier stock lasts longer on a cork board than thin copier paper. Save the heavier sheet for standing notices; use cheap letter paper for handouts that will be thrown out after the event.

digital.title: Print plus digital
digital.intro: Print and digital are not competing channels. The same facts should appear on the board, the flyer, social, and the website: one message, four channels.

facts.label: Lock the facts once
facts.content: Date, time, place, and who to contact must match everywhere. If one channel is wrong, members will trust none of them.

order.label: Post paper first when you can
order.content: Hand the flyer or pin the notice, then share a photo of the printed piece on social (with photo consent for anyone visible). Members who only see the feed still see the union on the wall.

qr.label: Let print send people digital
qr.content: A QR code on the flyer or board can open the live page, the RSVP, or the membership form when details change after you print.

digital.tip: If you only have time for one printed piece, make it the board notice or the flyer — then reuse the same headline in Graphic Maker so social does not invent a second message.

emailBroadcastGuide.title: Email & Member Outreach Guide
emailBroadcastGuide.subtitle: Copy-only invites and officer reminders. No marketing lists in UnionOps.

when.title: When email fits
when.content: Reach for email when members already trust that inbox — meeting notices, RSVPs, and reminders.

comms.title: Public Comms tools (copy / mailto)
comms.content: Document Generator, Board Notice, and Graphic Maker have a copy-only invite step. You paste into your inbox. UnionOps does not send mail.

hub.title: Officer Hub (separate surfaces)
hub.content: Officer Hub can draft membership-meeting reminder copy for officers. That is separate from the public invite email builders.

lists.title: What UnionOps does not do
lists.content: UnionOps does not keep member marketing lists, send automatic broadcasts, or handle dues or card payments. For newsletters, use your union’s approved mass-email provider and export the graphics from Comms separately.

checklist.title: Before you hit send
checklist.content: Make the subject line clear, put your local number in the body, and add a link or QR code for RSVPs. Keep sensitive case details out of any open broadcast.

shortFormGuide.title: Short-form Video Guide
shortFormGuide.subtitle: Film on a phone, keep member privacy, and send people to a real ask.
shortFormGuide.intro: UnionOps makes stills and captions. The camera and a phone editor make the clip. Use this page after Brand Kit and a social graphic, not instead of boards, print, or a closed Facebook group.

aspect.caption: Reels, Stories, and Shorts are tall. Graphic Maker is square or landscape today; crop a cover to Instagram Story size in Image Resizer, or export a 9:16 digital Solidarity Poster.

filming.title: Filming on a phone
filming.content: Hold the phone upright for Reels, Stories, and Shorts. Face a window, not a ceiling light. Speak close to the mic, or record a voiceover later in a quiet room. Shop floors and picket lines are loud; a short clip with on-screen text often beats a long take.

items.vertical: Film tall unless you know the post is a Facebook landscape.
items.light: Put faces toward a window or open shade. Avoid backlight that turns a speaker into a silhouette.
items.audio: If the floor is noisy, shoot silent footage and add a voiceover. Do not shout over machines.
items.background: Check who is behind the speaker. Faces, badges, and lanyards identify people too.
items.consent: Do not film grievances, medical spaces, or papers on a desk. Run Photo Consent before any member is on camera.

filming.consentTitle: Privacy is the same checklist as photos
filming.consentBody: Video is harder to crop after the fact. Get consent before you press record, including people clearly visible in the background.

editing.title: Edit on the phone you already have
editing.content: Trim, captions on screen, and a voiceover belong in a phone editor. UnionOps does not edit video. Start with the camera app. Named apps below are common; none of them run inside this site, and some upload footage to a cloud.
editing.stillsBody: Download a 9:16 cover or end card from Graphic Maker (Portrait) or Image Resizer (Instagram Story is 1080×1920), then drop it on the first and last frames. Copy a caption from the library. Point a QR or link at an Action Card, meeting notice, or your local website.

strategy.title: One ask, then a place to go
strategy.content: Open with who, what, and when in the first second. One action per clip. Start with the platform members already use. Many locals still live in a closed Facebook group. TikTok is optional, not a First week step. Skip weekly ranking tips; they go stale. Official how-to pages are in Sources below.

items.hook: Put the ask on screen as well as in speech, so the clip works with the sound off.
items.oneAsk: One meeting, one petition, or one website. Not all three.
items.handoff: Send people to something you already made: a QR, an Action Card, Captions plus Graphic Maker, or the Website Template.
items.platform: Do well on one channel before you split time across Instagram, YouTube Shorts, and TikTok.

checklist.title: Before you post
checklist.intro: Work through these once per clip, the same way First week walks boards then print then socials.

items.consent: Photo Consent is done, including background faces and location tags turned off.
items.cover: A tall cover or end card is exported (Graphic Maker Portrait, Image Resizer Story size, or a 9:16 Solidarity Poster).
items.caption: A caption is copied from the library and edited for this ask. Hashtags stay generic, without a union name.
items.alt: Alt text is drafted in Alt-Text Assistant for the cover still, then pasted into the platform field.
items.ask: The clip points at one action members can take this week.

photoConsentGuide.title: Photo Consent & Member Media
photoConsentGuide.subtitle: A short checklist to run before you post a member's photo.
photoConsentGuide.intro: Graphic Maker already gates consent on member photo upload. This page helps locals write a shared practice. Not legal advice.

why.title: Why it matters
why.content: Members should know how their image will be used before it appears on boards or socials.

checklist.title: Before you post
checklist.intro: Confirm each item before using a member photo in graphics, flyers, or board photos where faces are visible.

items.consent: You have written or verbal consent from the member
items.public: The member understands the photo will be posted publicly (or knows which audience will see it)
items.confidential: The photo and caption do not contain confidential workplace, grievance, medical, or bargaining information
items.group: For group photos, everyone who is clearly identifiable has been covered — or crop, blur, or choose a different image
items.minors: Photos of minors or dependents follow your local executive and union policy before you publish them
items.background: Faces in the background, badges, and lanyards are identifiable too — crop, wait, or get consent
items.location: Turn off location tags before you post, and do not film confidential casework or medical spaces
items.withdrawal: You know who to contact if a member later asks for the photo to be taken down

toolbox.title: In the Toolbox
toolbox.content: Use the Graphic Maker consent step, keep a simple local log, and prefer group shots when individuals have not consented. The same list applies before you film a Reel or Short.

workshop.title: Workshop tip

websiteGuide.title: Local Website Guide
websiteGuide.subtitle: Write a simple local site, download a ZIP, then put it online. A volunteer can do the tech steps.
websiteGuide.intro: Boards and socials move messages. A website holds who you are, who to email, and how to find you. Start with Part 1. Stop when the ZIP is on your computer.

glance.title: At a glance
glance.intro: Most locals only need Part 1. Stop when the ZIP is on your computer. Part 2 is for whoever will put those files on the internet.

part1.title: Write and download
part1.body: Gather a few facts, fill Website Template, and download the ZIP. No hosting account yet.

part2.title: Put it online
part2.body: Upload the ZIP to GitHub Pages for free. Skip this if a tech-savvy volunteer will do it.

part1.title: Planning and creating your site
part1.intro: Your job here is to write the content and download a ZIP. You can stop as soon as that file is on your computer.

part2.title: Publishing your site (the tech steps)
part2.intro: These steps put your downloaded ZIP on the internet so members can open a real web address.
part2.handoffTitle: Hand this off if you want
part2.handoff: Now that you have your website ZIP file, it needs to be put on the internet. If you are not comfortable with technical web setup, you can hand your downloaded ZIP file and this guide to a tech-savvy volunteer.

wordpress.title: Already on WordPress?
wordpress.body: Website Template can also download a WordPress theme. UnionOps does not support WordPress. Use that file only if someone already runs your site. Everyone else should stay with the GitHub Pages ZIP in this part.

squarespace.title: On Squarespace?
squarespace.body: Squarespace does not let you install a custom theme from a file. UnionOps cannot export a Squarespace template. If you already pay for Squarespace, rebuild the same sections in their editor using your colours, logo, and copy.

terms.title: A few words you will see

repository.meaning: An online folder on GitHub that holds your site files.

commit.meaning: Save the files you just uploaded, so GitHub keeps them.

deploy.meaning: Turn the site on so the public address starts working.

why.title: Why a local website
why.intro: A local website is not a news feed. It is the page members, media, and new hires still find months later.
why.tip: One clear web address beats a pile of outdated Docs and posts. Put it on boards, QR cards, signatures, and event graphics.

stable.label: A link that stays put
stable.content: Social feeds change and posts scroll away. A website keeps the contact email, officer names, and meeting basics in one place.

search.label: Search and credibility
search.content: Members, media, and employers search for your local. A simple public page beats a sparse Facebook profile alone.

control.label: Your copy, your timeline
control.content: You decide what stays live. No algorithm. The template opens the member’s email app so messages go straight to your inbox.

bareMinimum.title: Bare-minimum local site
bareMinimum.intro: A new member should answer these in under a minute: Who are you? Who runs the local? How do I reach you? Where do I follow updates?

about.title: About your local
about.content: Two short paragraphs: who you represent, where you work, and what you stand for. Orientation, not a novel.

officers.title: Executive officers
officers.content: Names and roles (president, steward coordinator, treasurer). Update after every election. Stale lists erode trust.

contact.title: Contact path
contact.content: One monitored local email, plus office address or steward hours if you have them. Prefer one inbox over five personal addresses that go stale.

social.title: Social or member channel
social.content: Link your Facebook group or other member channel. The site points there; social can point back for officers and email.

include.title: What belongs — and what does not
include.intro: Think in layers: always-on identity, campaign updates when active, and a short list of things that belong elsewhere.

always.label: Always on the site
always.content: About text, current officers, contact email, and your main social or group link.

whenActive.label: Add during active rounds
whenActive.content: A short bargaining or strike update paragraph, plus links to official parent-union resources. Not blow-by-blow chat logs.

optional.label: Optional later
optional.content: Meeting calendar, how to file a grievance overview, or links to CA highlights — only if someone will keep them current.

skip.label: Keep off the public site
skip.content: Member personal data, confidential strategy, unconsented photos, and anything your executive has not approved for public posting.

before.title: Before you open the template
before.intro: Five minutes of prep saves a broken-looking site. Gather these from Brand Kit and your local executive.
before.tip: When the site is live, save that web address in Brand Kit. QR cards and board posters can reuse it without retyping.

items.brand: Brand Kit set: local number, colours, and logo. The template picks those up automatically.
items.email: A monitored contact email the local actually checks.
items.officers: Current officer names and roles approved for the public site.
items.facebook: Facebook group address, or leave the field blank until you have one.

build.title: Build with Website Template
build.intro: Website Template fills a simple site in your browser. Preview it, then download a ZIP. You do not need a hosting account until someone publishes.
build.done: You can stop here. The ZIP on your computer is the file a volunteer needs to put the site online. Part 2 is next only if you are doing that yourself.

open.title: Open Website Template
open.content: Confirm Brand Kit colours and logo look right in the live preview before you type anything else.

fill.title: Fill the fields
fill.content: Add the name, tagline, about text, contact, Facebook, address, and officers. Replace every sample line before anyone publishes.

preview.title: Check the preview
preview.content: Read it like a new member: can you find who to email and who the president is without scrolling forever?

download.title: Download the ZIP
download.content: Save the ZIP to your computer. It holds the site pages, a short README with the same publish steps, and a CNAME.example file if you later add a custom domain.

deploy.title: Publish on GitHub Pages (free)
deploy.intro: GitHub Pages puts a simple site on the internet for free. You need a free GitHub account and about fifteen minutes the first time. The README inside the ZIP repeats these steps.
deploy.tip: The live address usually looks like https://yourusername.github.io/local243-site/. A GitHub organization can give a shorter address later. Either path works.
deploy.docsLead: If a GitHub screen looks different from this guide, use GitHub’s own help:

account.title: Create a free GitHub account
account.content: Sign up at github.com with an email the local can keep. Prefer a shared officer account over one personal login.

repo.title: Create a public repository (an online folder)
repo.content: Click New repository. Name it something clear, for example local243-site. Make it public so free GitHub Pages works. Skip adding a README if you will upload the ZIP next.

upload.title: Upload the ZIP contents, then commit (save)
upload.content: Unzip the file on your computer. Upload index.html, css/, js/, assets/, and README.md to the root of the online folder, not inside an extra folder. Click Commit changes to save the upload.

pages.title: Turn the site on in Settings → Pages
pages.content: Open Settings → Pages. Under Source, choose Deploy from a branch. Select main (or master) and / (root), then Save. That is the deploy step: GitHub starts building the public site.

wait.title: Wait for the live address
wait.content: GitHub usually finishes in a few minutes. Check Settings → Pages for the address, then open it in a private window to confirm links and the contact email.

domain.title: Optional: custom domain for advanced users
domain.intro: Skip this unless you already own a short domain (for example local243.org) and someone can change the address book at the company that sold it. The free github.io address works fine on boards and QR cards.
domain.tip: The ZIP includes a file called CNAME.example. Rename it to CNAME with no file extension, and put only your domain on the first line before you change DNS.
domain.docsLead: GitHub’s step-by-step for pointing a bought domain at Pages:

cname.title: Add a CNAME file (a one-line domain name)
cname.content: In the repository root (the online folder), add a file named CNAME with no file extension. Put only your domain on the first line, for example local243.org. Commit (save) it.

dns.title: Point the domain at GitHub (DNS)
dns.content: At the company where you bought the domain, add the records GitHub lists in its custom-domain help. DNS is the internet’s address book; changes can take minutes to a day.

enable.title: Enter the domain in Settings → Pages
enable.content: In Settings → Pages, type the custom domain, save, and wait until the secure lock (HTTPS) shows as ready. Then save the final address in Brand Kit.

maintain.title: Keep the site current
maintain.intro: A stale officer list is worse than no site. Assign ownership and a light refresh rhythm.

who.title: Who owns it
who.content: Name one site steward. Share the GitHub login or add a second trusted account so updates do not die when someone leaves.

when.title: When to update
when.content: After elections, contact changes, bargaining starts, or when a campaign needs a short public note.

how.title: How to edit
how.content: Easiest: update Website Template and upload a fresh ZIP. Or edit index.html in GitHub’s web editor for small fixes.

archive.title: What to remove
archive.content: Delete expired campaign blurbs and old meeting dates. Linking to a year-old “urgent” update teaches members to ignore the site.

pair.title: Pair the site with other channels
pair.intro: The website is the fourth First week channel, not a replacement for boards, print, or social.

boards.label: Union boards
boards.content: Put a site QR in the socials zone of the bare-minimum board so offline members still reach officers.

qr.label: QR link cards
qr.content: Print wallet or letter cards to the live address. Save the website link in Brand Kit first so tools can pull it.

social.label: Social posts
social.content: In bios and pinned posts, link the site for who you are and how to contact. Social for timely updates; site for stable facts.

brand.label: Brand Kit
brand.content: Keep colours and the website address in Brand Kit so regenerating the template or printing new QR materials stays consistent.

crisisGuide.title: Strike & Crisis Comms Guide
crisisGuide.subtitle: High-level guidance for local unions during strikes, bargaining, and workplace crises
crisisGuide.intro: This guide helps you keep local messaging calm and clear under pressure. Your local usually handles day-to-day Comms while your provincial or national union supports sector bargaining.

strike.title: Strike action
items: Confirm all public messaging with your local president and union servicing rep before posting
Designate one or two spokespersons - members and media should hear one consistent local voice
Post daily picket schedules, gate locations, and safety reminders using branded graphics from this toolbox
Share solidarity and member stories with consent - never post photos without permission
Use your Brand Kit colours; follow division or sector campaign materials when coordinating beyond the local
Do not share negotiation details, member home addresses, or internal strategy on public channels
Direct questions about pay, duties, and return-to-work to the local strike committee - not comment threads

bargaining.title: Bargaining and countdown
items: Build momentum with factual updates - job security, workload, wages, and member priorities
Use consistent hashtags and graphics so members recognize official local posts
Encourage members to wear union colours and attend information meetings - post times and locations early
Share only what the bargaining team has approved for public release
Remind members to avoid debating management claims in public comment sections
Link to official union bargaining pages when available rather than paraphrasing from memory

layoffs.title: Layoffs and restructuring
items: Acknowledge member anxiety - be empathetic, factual, and calm
Direct affected members to stewards, union servicing reps, and EAP resources
Do not speculate about outcomes - share only confirmed local and employer statements
Use quote cards from elected leaders to show a unified local voice
Document management communications offline for grievance and consultation records
Avoid naming individuals at risk unless they have asked to be identified publicly

management.title: Management pushback and misinformation
items: Respond with facts and collective agreement language - never personal attacks
If management posts misinformation, publish one brief correction and pin it if needed
Escalate harassment, threats, or surveillance concerns to your union servicing rep immediately
Do not engage in prolonged public arguments with management accounts
Keep sensitive member issues in steward channels, not public posts
Screenshot problematic employer posts for the local executive and servicing rep

escalation.title: When to escalate
items: Media inquiries - route to your designated spokesperson or union communications
Legal threats, injunctions, or employer letters about conduct - executive and servicing rep immediately
Member safety incidents on the line or in the workplace - follow local emergency protocols first
Leaked confidential documents or suspected bad-faith bargaining - do not post; alert leadership
Viral misinformation about your local - coordinate a single correction rather than multiple replies

dfrGuide.title: Duty of Fair Representation
dfrGuide.subtitle: Foundational literacy for stewards and local officers
dfrGuide.intro: Duty of fair representation is the union’s duty to represent each member fairly. Missed deadlines and silent refusals are common risk points. This guide is orientation, not legal advice.

disclaimer.title: Not legal advice
disclaimer.body: Not legal advice. Confirm procedure with your local officers and counsel.

whatItMeans.title: What DFR means in practice
whatItMeans.content: DFR means the union must handle representation without bad faith, discrimination, or arbitrary refusal.
items: Investigate complaints promptly and document what you did
Communicate status updates to the member in plain language
Apply the collective agreement consistently across similar cases
Escalate early when deadlines, complexity, or conflict of interest appear

legalTest.title: The “arbitrary / discriminatory / bad faith” test
legalTest.content: Courts look for honesty of purpose, non-discrimination, and a non-arbitrary process. Perfect outcomes are not required.
items: Arbitrary — rubber-stamping a refusal, never reading the file, missing a known deadline
Discriminatory — treating members differently because of protected grounds or personal dislike
Bad faith — lying to the member, burying evidence, or advancing a personal agenda
Honest disagreement with a member after a real investigation is usually not a DFR breach

failureModes.title: Common failure modes
failureModes.content: Most DFR complaints grow from silence and missed clocks, not malice. Leave a paper trail of serious consideration.
items: Missed Step / referral deadlines in the collective agreement
No investigation notes, interviews, or document requests on file
No written explanation when declining to advance a grievance
Promising outcomes you cannot control (“we will win this”)
Mixing personal conflict with representation decisions

practice.title: Steward and officer practice checklist
practice.content: Hub grievance tools track steps and dates. The CA and your servicing rep stay authoritative. When unsure, document the question and escalate.
items: Log the member’s concern the same day you hear it
Put every CA deadline in your calendar, counted forward from the triggering event
Confirm extension agreements in writing
Keep confidential notes internal — never on public social channels
If you cannot act fairly (conflict), hand the file to another officer

hub.body: Officer Hub grievance tools help with dates and handoffs. They do not replace legal judgment.

seniorityGuide.title: Seniority & bumping playbook
seniorityGuide.subtitle: Seniority worksheets for bumping files. Aid only.
seniorityGuide.intro: Bumping files turn on seniority dates, classification boundaries, and posting rules. Use the worksheet to organize facts. Verify against your CA.

disclaimer.title: Not legal advice. Aid only.
disclaimer.body: Not a calculator and not legal advice. Confirm dates and rights against the CA and local practice.

compare.title: Worked example: comparing seniority
compare.content: Start with two members and one target role. Write seniority date, classification, and status on one sheet before debating.
items: List Member A and Member B with seniority date (YYYY-MM-DD) and classification
Confirm which date the CA uses — continuous service, classification seniority, or another clock
Note ties and how your CA breaks them (e.g. earlier hire number, draw)
Only then compare qualifications, hours, and posting eligibility against the CA language

cascade.title: Cascading displacement walk-through
cascade.content: A bump can displace another member, who may bump further. Map the chain before the committee votes.
items: Draw the chain: vacancy → first bumper → displaced incumbent → next bump (if any)
Stop when the CA says the chain ends (classification floor, probation, temporary status)
Flag anyone who cannot bump (wrong classification, insufficient seniority, refused options)
Record each step in the committee log with dates and CA articles cited

pitfalls.title: Common pitfalls
pitfalls.content: Most committee errors come from mixing clocks or ignoring boundaries the CA already defines.
items: Posting date vs. seniority date — do not treat a vacancy posting date as someone’s seniority
Classification boundaries — FT/PT or support-staff collections may not bump across freely
Probationary or temporary status — confirm bumping rights before ranking someone
Assuming “earlier date always wins” without reading the CA’s tie-break and ability language

worksheet.title: Paper worksheet (print or copy)
worksheet.content: Use this column layout on a blank page or spreadsheet during the meeting. Keep one copy in the case file.
items: Columns: Member ref · Seniority date · Classification · Current position · Target / bump claim · Eligible? (Y/N/?) · Notes / CA article
Rows: one per person in the chain, plus a blank row for alternate candidates
Footer: session date, chair, decision summary, and link to the Officer Hub bumping case ID
worksheet.exportHint: Opens Document Generator with a blank branded seniority grid ready to export.

hub.body: In the Officer Hub, College Bumping keeps your notes, PDF comparisons, and sessions in one place. Treat any ranking aid as a double-check, and re-run the paper worksheet if a result surprises you.

rightToRefuseGuide.title: Right to refuse unsafe work
rightToRefuseGuide.subtitle: OHSA s.43 refusal steps for stewards and JHSC members. Not legal advice.
rightToRefuseGuide.intro: Summary of the Ontario OHSA s.43 refusal procedure for college-sector stewards and JHSC members. Confirm against current legislation.

disclaimer.title: Not legal advice
disclaimer.body: Procedure overview only. Confirm with JHSC practice, local officers, and current OHSA text.

ontarioScope.title: Ontario scope (read this first)
ontarioScope.content: OHSA s.43 covers most provincially regulated Ontario workplaces, with exceptions. Verify coverage for your workplace type before advising.
items: Label this guide Ontario-only in any local training materials you reprint
Federal workplaces and other provinces follow different refusal frameworks
Some workers have modified rights — check current OHSA text and ministry materials
Union representation supports the member; it does not replace JHSC or ministry roles

procedure.title: Step-by-step refusal (report)
procedure.content: A worker who believes work is likely to endanger them (or another) may refuse. Report promptly. Do not walk out in silence.
items: Worker promptly reports the circumstances to the supervisor / employer
Worker remains in a safe place nearby and available for investigation steps
Worker may be accompanied by a JHSC worker member or union health-and-safety rep where the Act provides
Employer investigates in the presence of the worker and the worker representative

investigation.title: If the worker still refuses
investigation.content: When the danger is not resolved to the worker’s satisfaction, the matter escalates beyond the internal investigation.
items: Notify a Ministry of Labour inspector — the employer or worker (or JHSC member) can trigger this
Inspector investigates and decides whether the refusal is likely to endanger
Do not coach members to invent hazards — facts, dates, and witnesses matter
Keep notes of times, who was present, and what was said for the local file

reassignment.title: Work reassignment rules (high level)
reassignment.content: While a refusal is live, employers generally cannot assign the same work to another worker without informing them, subject to OHSA. Verify current Act language before advising.
items: Other workers assigned the work must be informed of the refusal and reasons
The refusing worker is typically paid pending the investigation outcome, subject to Act rules
Reprisals for exercising OHSA rights are prohibited — escalate suspected reprisals immediately
Post current JHSC contacts and hazard-reporting steps on the union board

boards.body: Keep JHSC contacts and a short hazard / refusal strip on the board. Link QR posters to official e-Laws OHSA text, not outdated photocopies.

installPage.title: Install UnionOps on your desktop
installPage.intro: On supported browsers you can install UnionOps as an app window. No app store and no extra download beyond the browser.
installPage.whereBody: Use unionops.org (not www). It works best in Chrome or Edge on a computer and in Safari on iPhone or iPad. On Android, use Chrome when it offers Install app.
installPage.chromeStep1: Open https://unionops.org in Chrome, Edge, or Brave.
installPage.chromeStep2: After a short visit, use Install in the address bar, or the browser menu: Install app / Install UnionOps.
installPage.chromeStep3: Confirm. UnionOps opens in its own window with the offline shell for public pages you last loaded. Missing Install? You may already be in the installed app.
installPage.androidBody: In the Chrome menu, tap Install app. If you only see “Add to Home screen,” that just makes a shortcut, not the full app — use Install whenever it shows up.
installPage.safariBody: Safari never shows an automatic install prompt. On iPhone or iPad: Share, then Add to Home Screen.
installPage.limitsOffline: Installed app windows still need network for first load and some Hub features.
installPage.limitsNetwork: Grievance, bumping, and other Officer Hub modules still need a signed-in session and a network connection when you work live.
installPage.limitsBrand: The installed window uses your Brand Kit's main colour. After you change colours, reopen the app (or reinstall it once) if your device still shows the old icon or title bar.
installPage.limitsNoStore: There is no App Store or Microsoft Store listing, because installing uses your browser's own app-install feature.

workshopGuide.title: From Scratch to Solidarity: Launching Your Local's Social Media
workshopGuide.subtitle: A beginner hour for volunteer executives: strategy, a local logo, example posts, graphics, quote cards, and a simple website ZIP.
workshopGuide.intro: Project this page or follow it on your own device. The numbered agenda is a 45 to 60 minute lunch-and-learn. Notes marked Facilitator are for the person at the front; Do this is for everyone else.
workshopGuide.audienceFacilitator: Share this browser tab, not the whole desktop. Use Quick links instead of typing addresses. Zoom to about 110 percent so type reads from the back of the room.
workshopGuide.audienceAttendee: Keep this page open. When a tool is named, tap the matching Quick link and work in the same browser. Files you make stay on this device; you do not need an account.
workshopGuide.prereqIntro: Have these ready before the hour starts so the first download is yours, not a demo.

prereq.device: A laptop, tablet, or phone with a current browser. A laptop is easier for typing; a phone is enough to follow along.
prereq.logo: A digital copy of your local logo if you have one (PNG, JPG, or SVG). If you do not, Logo Builder makes a starter during the identity step.
prereq.colours: A rough idea of your local's colours, from letterhead, a banner, or a printed notice. Exact colour codes are optional.
prereq.number: Your local number, if it appears on your materials.
prereq.prompt: Optional: one real announcement or quote you might post this week, so the practice is a real post, not a placeholder.

workshopGuide.demoLead: Keep this box in view. Tap a tool when the agenda names it. Same five stops as the 20-minute live demo.
workshopGuide.demoNote: Strategy lives on First week, not on these numbered stops. The live path is Logo Builder, Social Examples, Graphic Maker, Quote Card, then Website Template. Print and Board Notice stay on First week.
workshopGuide.outlineIntro: Times add up to about 50 minutes, with room for questions. If you have a full hour, linger on Graphic Maker. If you have 45 minutes, keep the downloads moving.

strategy.title: High-level social media strategy
strategy.do: Listen for three essentials: platforms you can sustain, a shared account that is not a personal account, and a posting rhythm that will not burn out the executive. First week is the written plan you leave with.
strategy.facilitator: Open First week, then The Blueprint. Do not start inside a maker yet. Ask who holds the passwords today.

identity.title: Creating your identity
identity.do: Open Logo Builder. Set your local number and colours if needed, generate a circular logo, and download the PNG. This is the file you take home.
identity.facilitator: If the kit is empty, import the demo Brand Kit first. Share Logo Builder, not Brand Kit, as the identity beat. Show the PNG download succeeding.

inspiration.title: Finding inspiration
inspiration.do: Open Social Examples. Browse strike, AGM, and member-spotlight layouts so you are not staring at a blank screen. Tap one example to seed Graphic Maker when the next block starts.
inspiration.facilitator: This is the example gallery. Do not open Board Notice Maker unless someone asks about cork boards; point to the Union Boards guide instead.

media.title: Generating media content
media.do: Open Graphic Maker, pick a preset, and download a PNG. Then make a Quote Card. Graphic Maker is Facebook landscape and Instagram square; Image Resizer is how you hit other crops.
media.facilitator: Pause on the photo consent dialog. Do not demo Pulse Poll publish. If a download fails, show a PNG you saved before the session. Skip Captions unless minutes remain.

close.title: Leave with a plan
close.do: You should have a logo PNG, one graphic, a quote card, and a Website Template ZIP. Open First week for the written plan. The practice checklist on Comms Resources is homework, not extra talking time.
close.facilitator: Thank people. Show the ZIP download succeeding. Point to Comms Resources and stop on time. Skip GitHub Pages unless someone asks.

workshopGuide.wrapIntro: Do these before the week is out, while the files are still on this device.

wrap.bookmark: Bookmark Brand Kit in this browser so your colours are still here when you come back. If you share the computer, download the Brand Kit file from Brand Kit and keep it with your local records.
wrap.logo: Keep the Logo Builder PNG with your local records, and use it on the Facebook cover only after whoever must approve identity has said yes.
wrap.post: Open the First week roadmap and attempt your first real post using the graphic and quote card you made today.
wrap.website: Open Website Template and download the ZIP when you want a simple local page you can host later.
wrap.checklist: When you have a quiet half hour, work through the practice checklist on Comms Resources.

workshopGuide.wrapFacilitator: Thank people. Remind them public Comms stay on the device. If something broke, the Feedback page on this site takes a note without a member mailing list.

privacyPage.title: Privacy Policy
privacyPage.subtitle: Last updated: July 2026
privacyPage.leadBodyHub: Comms graphics and brand settings stay on your device. The Officer Hub runs on the host that operates it, and that operator is responsible for the data it holds.
privacyPage.leadBodyCommsOnly: Public Comms are local-first: graphics and brand settings stay on your device. An Officer Hub for casework is not part of the public launch yet.
privacyPage.comms1: Image processing, templates, and file preparation happen in your browser
privacyPage.comms2: Brand kit settings are stored in browser local storage
privacyPage.comms3: No analytics, tracking cookies, or third-party ad scripts
privacyPage.comms4: Member photos used in graphics are not uploaded to UnionOps servers by the Comms tools
privacyPage.hubIntro: When you sign in, that Hub stores your session and case records. Demo setups may lose data on restart; a real deployment keeps each union's records secure and separate.
privacyPage.hubSelfHost: If you self-host (CapRover / Docker), you are the data controller. Prefer Canadian hosting for confidential modules. Set a unique AUTH_SECRET. Never use demo passwords for real casework.
privacyPage.hubHybrid: Hybrid export passphrases stay in the browser. They are not sent to the server in the encrypt flow.
privacyPage.hubDemo: Demo accounts exist for workshops and CI only, not for live confidential files.
privacyPage.ontarioHub: Designed around PIPEDA and, where applicable, FIPPA. Comms stay on-device. Hub hosts must apply access control, retention, and breach practices for labour records.
privacyPage.ontarioCommsOnly: UnionOps follows Canada privacy principles, including PIPEDA and, where applicable, FIPPA. Comms tools minimize collection by keeping work on-device.
privacyPage.contactBody: UnionOps is stewarded by Ryan Morris. For questions about this policy, contact your local communications chair or see Support.
privacyPage.responsibilitiesBody: You remain responsible for photo consent and for posts and case handling that match your local policies and CA. Not legal advice.
privacyPage.installBody: Supported browsers can install UnionOps as an app window. Offline shell stays on-device; Hub case data still needs a network when live.
privacyPage.siteFeedbackBody: If you send a note from the feedback page, this host stores the text and any optional name or email you include, so the operator can improve UnionOps. Optional email is for a reply only, never a mailing list. You can ask the operator to delete your note.
